title: A cathedral to song
gist: Alan Rusbridger reviews the 2026 Three Choirs Festival's opening night at Gloucester Cathedral — Adrian Partington conducting Elgar's Symphony No 1 and Walton's Belshazzar's Feast with the Philharmonia — and argues the festival, often claimed the world's oldest, is in the rudest health and has outgrown its historic billing as a provincial event. Along the way he notes that two works written only 23 years apart inhabit entirely different harmonic universes, an implicit claim that musical style once moved far faster than it does today.

insights.claim: The Three Choirs Festival, often claimed to be the oldest music festival in the world, is in the rudest of health, with Gloucester Cathedral's nave full to bursting on opening night of the 2026 edition.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Live classical demand at heritage venues is holding up — a counterpoint to the standard decline narrative around orchestral audiences.
insights.quote: A rousing climax so loud it practically blew the Norman roof off.
insights.locator: The cathedral nave full to bursting point

insights.claim: A contemporaneous Hereford Times account of the 1909 festival — the 186th meeting of the three choirs — called it one of the leading festivals in the provinces, a label Rusbridger says should now be upgraded to leading in the world.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Regional UK cultural institutions can hold globally competitive positioning; useful framing for cultural tourism and heritage-venue economics.

insights.claim: The 2026 festival rotates through Gloucester, Hereford and Worcester, with Gloucester hosting this year and running until 1st August.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: The rotating-venue model spreads audience and infrastructure load across three cathedral cities rather than concentrating it.

themes.theme: Pace of stylistic change in music

insights.claim: Elgar's Symphony No 1 and Walton's Belshazzar's Feast are separated by just 23 years yet inhabit entirely different emotional and harmonic universes, whereas a listener today would struggle to distinguish a piece written in 2003 from one written now.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: An argument that stylistic innovation in classical composition has effectively stalled over the past two decades — a cultural-stagnation datapoint.
insights.quote: Could you, on a blind listening, spot a piece written in 2003 against one written today?
insights.locator: The two pieces were separated by just 23 years

insights.claim: Elgar's Symphony No 1 was written six years before the First World War and Walton's Belshazzar's Feast was premiered in Leeds Town Hall in 1931, with Elgar himself conducting his symphony at the Three Choirs Festival in Hereford in 1909.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Programming that pairs works with direct festival provenance builds institutional narrative — a repeatable device for heritage arts marketing.
insights.locator: Elgar conducted his symphony at the Three Choirs Festival

insights.claim: Belshazzar's Feast was banned from the Three Choirs Festival for 25 years after the Times music critic HC Colles denounced it as 'stark Judaism from first to last', with Worcester organist Ivor Atkins helping enforce the exclusion.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A concrete case of gatekeeper criticism suppressing a now-canonical work for a generation — a caution about how institutional taste-making misprices new output.
insights.quote: denouncing it as “stark Judaism from first to last”
insights.locator: Belshazzar’s Feast had a rockier history with the festival

themes.theme: Acoustics and conducting craft at Gloucester

insights.claim: Gloucester Cathedral's cavernous nave carries roughly three full beats of echo after the chorus shout of 'Slain!' in Belshazzar's Feast, forcing tempo choices that preserve clear textures in fast passages.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Venue acoustics function as a binding constraint on repertoire and interpretation — resident-conductor knowledge is a genuine, non-transferable asset.
insights.quote: I counted another three full beats before the echo disappeared.
insights.locator: There’s a notorious moment in the Walton

insights.claim: Adrian Partington, Gloucester's director of music since 2008 and primarily a choral conductor, drew a memorable Elgar symphony out of the Philharmonia orchestra, showing that choral specialists can deliver large-scale orchestral repertoire.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Long tenure in a specific venue may matter more than orchestral specialism for concert quality — an argument for continuity in artistic leadership.
insights.locator: Partington is mainly a choral conductor

insights.claim: The Walton performance deployed two brass bands in antiphonal competition from the north and south transepts, a baritone solo from David Stout, and opened with a fanfare by Gavin Higgins.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Spatial staging exploits cathedral architecture as a production asset that concert halls cannot replicate.
insights.quote: with two brass bands in exuberant antiphonal competition from north and south transepts
